    Tech Report: We Tested the Shimano Sustain FK Spinning Reel in Fresh and Salt Water

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
    • The market is cluttered with spinning reels, and sorting through them to find one that meets specific needs can be a headache.
    • In a recent development, after all, why spend almost $400 on a 2500-size spinning reel that looks and feels about the same in hand as one that costs a quarter of the price?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    The market is cluttered with spinning reels, and sorting through them to find one that meets specific needs can be a headache. That is especially true in light-tackle and inshore fishing, easily the most popular market for spinning reel manufacturers. At first glance, many reels in the 2500-size class, the standard size for this category, look identical. Appearances can be deceiving, though, and knowing how and where you initiative to use a reel matters more in this class than in most others.

    In a recent development, after all, why spend almost $400 on a 2500-size spinning reel that looks and feels about the same in hand as one that costs a quarter of the price? It turns out there are plenty of reasons, and Shimano makes the case for most of them with its updated Sustain FK series.

    The Sustain FK gets its strength and light weight from Hagane metal body technology, a process of cold-forging rigid metals such as aluminum and magnesium. As part of Shimano’s MagnumLite series, the metal frame is also paired with an ultralight CI4+ carbon rotor. The result is a reel that feels solid and strong where it should, while staying smooth and light in use.

    It has been revealed that the Sustain FK uses DuraCross, a relatively upcoming drag system from Shimano. The idea is that precisely layered materials give the reel a smoother, longer-lasting drag than older materials such as felt. Inside, the reel uses S A-RB bearings, which are shielded and rust-resistant to keep debris out. That adds a layer of protection against sand and salt, which helps keep the reel working in the saltwater conditions it was built for. Shimano also uses what it calls X-Protect, essentially a labyrinth of barriers that makes it far more difficult for salt water or grit to reach the interior of the reel.

    No reel is invincible to the hazards of extended saltwater use, but the Sustain FK has a number of features that make it well suited to the task. Corrosion-resistant materials in the frame and gearing, S A-RB sealed bearings and Shimano’s X-Protect design give this reel several strong defenses against the wear and tear of frequent saltwater exposure. Shimano also pairs the DuraCross drag with its Rigid Support Drag to give this small reel a surprisingly strong backbone. The DuraCross drag in particular is a serious upgrade from the standard felt or carbon washers of previous models.

    In a recent development, shimano offers a one-year service warranty on its reels, including the Sustain FK. After that year, you can still send the reel in for service, and Shimano will usually inspect it and tell you the cost before doing the work. Experiences vary, but I’ve sent reels to Shimano countless times over the years and have found its warranty and service system easy to deal with and accommodating.

    Shimano touts the Sustain FK as a crossover reel for fresh water and inshore salt water, with a combination of light finesse and rigid durability suited to both. With that in mind, I fished it in a wide range of environments over the course of a year, from bass fishing on large lakes and rivers with a variety of techniques to inshore saltwater fishing that ranged from shallow flats to deep near-shore jigging. The goal was to see whether it could stand up to the all-purpose abuse dished out by hardcore anglers nationwide while still delivering the refinement and finesse expected of a top-end spinning reel in the age of forward-facing sonar. Fishing from both boats and kayaks, I caught largemouth and smallmouth bass, redfish, striped bass and speckled trout.

    According to recent reports, corrosion will always be the No. 1 concern when using any reel in salt water, especially one as small and lightweight as the Sustain FK 2500. To get a proper idea of how this reel holds up, I spent the better part of a year fishing with it from my kayak in places like Chesapeake Bay and Laguna Madre in Texas.

    A kayak is a great place to test how a reel holds up to the salt because the reel gets so much more direct exposure. Spray tends to reach reels sitting in kayak rod holders, and splashing water is much closer to your gear during high-intensity moments like fighting fish or navigating heavy current. Then there are the times anglers (myself included) accidentally submerge their gear when they aren’t paying attention.

    Recent findings suggest that so, how did the Sustain FK hold up? Remarkably well, I’m pleased to say. After roughly eight months of consistent, heavy saltwater use, the reel is still about as smooth as the day I opened it. It needs some basic maintenance, such as a freshwater rinse and a coat of reel oil now and then, but overall, I’m very impressed.

    Recent findings suggest that smoothness matters, but a viable saltwater spinning reel needs a lot more than that. Saltwater game fish are bigger, stronger and live in harsher environments than most freshwater species, and a light spinning reel needs the backbone to stand up to that kind of abuse regularly without losing function. This is where the Sustain FK impressed me most. I intentionally used it in situations where the odds of hooking fish well outside its class were high, and I was able to fight and land everything from bull redfish to large striped bass around heavy cover without the reel bending or warping. The drag may be the reel’s best feature. It stayed smooth and clean during long runs that would have fried the drag on many reels in its class. The Rigid Support system was just as impressive. A reel this light will typically flex under that much strain, but the Sustain FK stayed rigid and smooth.

    Ultimately, the Sustain FK passed every saltwater test with flying colors.

    Being able to land saltwater fish well outside its intended class is great, but a high-end spinning reel should perform best at what it is intended for. That means no hiccups with anti-reverse or drag slippage, and handling line twist and line lay well. Today, it also means having the fine-tuning required for the extremely finesse-oriented game of fishing with forward-facing sonar. Love it or hate it, forward-facing sonar has become a standard part of professional angling, especially in the bass world.

    With all that in mind, I used the Sustain FK for a wide range of freshwater applications. It performed well in traditional settings like fishing light jigs for river smallmouth bass and crappie, but that’s admittedly not a demanding test. Where this reel really shone was targeting bass on large, deep lakes where finesse and control at depth were key. Fishing with and without forward-facing sonar, I was impressed with the amount of control I could keep on the lure. From jerkbaits to small soft plastics, it never faltered with line management or fine-tuned movements.

    Sources indicate that the anti-twist fin that Shimano builds into the line roller on many of its high-end reels may sound like a gimmick, but trust me, it makes a substantial difference. There’s not much worse than light braid twisting while you try to make long casts or present a bait at depth. It can cause wind knots and a host of other complications. Throughout testing, the line on this reel never kinked, twisted or laid poorly on the spool.

    Recent findings suggest that finally, while the smooth, strong drag is great in salt water, the ability to fine-tune it is even more impressive for finesse fishing in fresh water. Getting a solid hook set in deep water on leader as light as 6-pound test can be critical for serious anglers, and that requires a drag that doesn’t slip or freeze up. The Sustain FK drag can be adjusted to the most minute settings, allowing for just the right resistance when setting the hook or playing fish on light line.

    Industry observers note that I can’t remember using a reel that was as much at home fishing ultralight for crappie and perch as it was fishing a marsh for drag-ripping bull redfish and striped bass. I may be in the minority, but I love having a lightweight 2500-size spinning reel that pulls double duty as both my favorite freshwater finesse setup and my favorite inshore spinning rig. The crossover ability of the Sustain FK is fantastic. It’s not just a good freshwater reel that’s decent in the salt, or a saltwater reel that’s light enough to use in fresh water. It’s at the top of its game in both.

    The Sustain FK is an exceptional reel, so finding areas for improvement is difficult. The most obvious is the price. The engineering and performance can justify it, but there’s no denying that nearly $400 for a light spinning reel is steep for the average angler. There are plenty of equally light and smooth spinning reels on the market for far less. Those reels may not match the Sustain FK’s quality and durability across the board, but those features probably don’t matter as much to many freshwater or casual inshore anglers.

    Sources indicate that if you’re looking for a light-tackle spinning reel that’s durable and strong while still being incredibly smooth and light, the Sustain FK is the ideal choice. It’s comfortable to fish in both fresh and salt water, with the refinement needed for the most finesse-oriented applications.

    This review focused on the 2500, but the Sustain FK presently comes in sizes from 2500 through 5000. The limited size range is a downside, but given that this reel is designed for such a specific level of performance, it makes sense to offer it only in sizes that don’t compromise that.

    Read Next: The Best Fishing Kayaks.

    Recent findings suggest that although the price tag isn’t cheap, this reel is the complete package for serious anglers who want professional-grade performance from their gear. Tournament bass anglers and hardcore inshore anglers alike will appreciate the refinement the Sustain FK delivers over similar-size, budget-friendly options.

    Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the U.S.
    • The complex and winding 400-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act focuses on lowering energy costs, something both Republicans and Democrats have championed and and that helped drive Democratic gains in the midterm elections.
    • Recent findings suggest that BAAJA is largely focused on permitting reform, something the country hasn’t tackled in decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the U.S. Senate plans to vote this week on a bill aimed at easing America’s affordability crisis and fighting climate change that hunting and fishing groups worry will also erode many of the nation’s bedrock conservation laws.

    The complex and winding 400-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act focuses on lowering energy costs, something both Republicans and Democrats have championed and and that helped drive Democratic gains in the midterm elections. BAAJA also, however, ties jobs and household bills with curtailing public-lands protections. And in a twist that’s perplexing many conservation groups, the bill is co-sponsored by Sens. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Mike Lee (R-Utah), two lawmakers known for being on nearly opposite ends of the public-lands spectrum.

    Recent findings suggest that BAAJA is largely focused on permitting reform, something the country hasn’t tackled in decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. In practice, the legislation would raise the standard for whether projects approved by one administration can be revoked by a future administration.

    Recent findings suggest that that means an industrial solar project permitted by one president, for example, could not be stymied by a future president intent on preventing renewables. It also speeds up permitting processes and cuts red tape for everything from energy projects to landscape-scale changes like prescribed fire.

    Recent findings suggest that but sportsmen and conservationists say the bill would not just expedite climate or environmentally friendly projects. BAAJA would also make it much harder — or potentially impossible — for an administration to overturn leases or approvals for projects as controversial as hyperscale data centers on public lands or mines in the same watersheds as sensitive wilderness areas. It’s a bill that prioritizes development, many observers say, at the cost of the very “red tape” that has been responsible for conserving many of the country’s most priceless fish, wildlife, and wild places.

    It has been revealed that “I understand this is a big, bipartisan bill — it has some things in it I would rather it not have.     “We need to be exceptionally aware of the implications of this bill, which could be that a lot of these really beloved places could have projects many communities have worked really hard to oppose cemented into place.”.

    An Idaho Fish and Game commissioner just made a deal to avoid poaching and trespassing charges related to an illegal elk hunt last season.

    On Nov. 9 eastern Idaho’s representative, Brody Harshbarger, agreed to plead guilty to two of seven charges of wildlife violations in exchange for having the remaining charges dropped.

    Recent findings suggest that his guilty pleas are for hunting without a tag and shooting across the road, according to local news outlets. The dismissed charges include two for poaching, trespass, motorized aid and failure to retrieve game. Both of the killed animals were bull elk, one antlerless and the other a 6×6 which was on private property. Harshbarger was accompanied by another man, Eric Murphy, at the time.

    Related: Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Charged with Poaching Elk, Trespassing, Says He’ll ‘Voluntarily Postpone’ Duties.

    Industry observers note that “Neither Brody Harshbarger nor Eric Murphy called the landowners to request permission to retrieve the six-point bull and did not make a reasonable effort to retrieve the six-point bull,” according to investigation documents obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun. “Neither individual had permission to be shooting onto the private property in violation of Idaho Code.”.

    It has been revealed that harshbarger had already filled his elk tag the weekend before the two bulls were shot. His hometown, Ashton, is in the same county where the violations took place. That same county, Fremont, borders Yellowstone National Park and is in the region Harshbarger represents on the state’s seven-person commission. That commission sets statewide hunting, fishing, and trapping seasons plus bag limits and other regulations based on recommendations and research supplied by Idaho Department of Fish and Game scientists.

    Each member of the commission, most often a resident hunter and/or fisherman, is appointed by the governor for a term of four years with a two-term maximum. The commission meets at least four times a year. Harshbarger hasn’t attended those meetings since his case opened after a tip received through the department’s Citizens Against Poaching in December. He hasn’t resigned and the Governor hasn’t dismissed him, but his profile has been removed from the commission’s website.

    “The Governor’s office is aware of Commissioner Harshbarger’s plea agreement,” Gov. Brad Little’s spokeswoman Emily Callihan told the Sun. “Gov. Little will be working with the Idaho Department of Fish and Game and stakeholders in the coming days to ensure the responsibilities of the position are fulfilled.”.

    Recent findings suggest that harshbarger was appointed to the commission in 2024. His sentencing for illegal activities in 2025 is scheduled for Dec. 9. With the new plea deal and the number of charges reduced, the fine is expected to be $500 plus a one-year loss of hunting privileges.

    Read Next: DNA Evidence Helps Convict Serial Poacher, Who Forfeited 2 Vehicles and Hunting Privileges for Life.

    Industry observers note that CAP received 1,596 calls about illegal wildlife-related activity in 2025, the highest on record since an annual total started rolling in 2019. A tip about a poached elk that leads to an arrest is worth $400. CAP rewarded tipsters more than $23,000 in 2025.

    One summer evening, I was hiking a trail near Marias Pass in Glacier National Park, returning to the car after a few hours of wildlife photography at a lake— nothing but deer and mosquitoes to show for it—when I noticed something blondish-brown moving toward me. It barely registered. I felt relaxed, though, truthfully, I’m never fully relaxed.

    And then we were on top of each other.

    Sources indicate that A grizzly cub, significant as an overgrown Saint Bernard. I was fascinated—until reality hit. The mother wouldn’t be far behind.

    “Hey, bear,” I shouted, my voice cracking. The cub woofed an alarm and took off to my left, a dark blur swallowed by the forest.

    I turned toward the trail ahead. And—boom—there she was. Running at me, big and fast and flat to the ground.

    Recent findings suggest that I grabbed the bear spray strapped to my chest, fumbled the can free, and held it out like a pistol. She closed in. I could see the whites.

    #21944. Jeff Sturgis’ Secrets for Hunting Massive Whitetail Bucks

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1091 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

    Jeff Sturgis’ Secrets for Hunting Massive Whitetail Bucks

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1091 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, jeff Sturgis has made a name for himself by helping deer hunters and property owners better understand habitat and high-level hunting strategies.
    • Recent findings suggest that this summer, I got to visit Sturgis’ property and get a high-level overview of how he thinks about habitat and targeting mature bucks.
    • Whether or not you are able to build these exact setups on your own hunting area, there are some key lessons you can learn from him.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, jeff Sturgis has made a name for himself by helping deer hunters and property owners better understand habitat and high-level hunting strategies. He’s honed these strategies through decades of hard hunting and consulting on his clients’ properties. He’s also tested them on his own 170-acre property in the bluff country of southern Minnesota (you can follow him on his YouTube channel, Whitetail Habitat Solutions).

    Recent findings suggest that this summer, I got to visit Sturgis’ property and get a high-level overview of how he thinks about habitat and targeting mature bucks. In the video above, Sturgis runs through his five favorite setups and explains how he hunts them. Some of these setups take an immense amount of work and expense to develop. Others require minimal habitat work but a deep understanding of deer behavior.

    Whether or not you are able to build these exact setups on your own hunting area, there are some key lessons you can learn from him.

    In a recent development, everyone talks about “buck bedding areas” but many hunters have only a vague understanding of them. The important point, Sturgis notes, is that bucks do not like to bed near a lot of commotion, and that includes commotion from other deer. For example, does will often bed near major food sources. It’s convenient for them to get up from their bed and stroll right into a large food plot or ag field.

    Sources indicate that mature bucks don’t like to bed around a mass of other deer. So buck beds will be found farther away from main food sources — even if there is prime bedding habitat right by those food sources. So just because you’re seeing a lot of does and young bucks in an area doesn’t mean it’s a good spot for mature bucks. In fact, it could mean the opposite.

    By crossing off areas where mature bucks won’t bed — again, areas with high pressure and activity — you can narrow down where they will bed. Sturgis isn’t afraid to hunt near buck bedding areas, but he does so sparingly. And when he does, he often takes his target buck.

    Sources indicate that when you see deer consistently coming to a significant food plot or agricultural field during daylight hours, it’s tempting to just hunt that major food source. Sturgis will hunt the big “holding plot” on his property, but only when he’s able to do so without spooking deer. He’s got a Redneck blind at the edge of the plot, which has an access route that is completely blocked by screening cover. He can get into and out of the blind with deer in the field — and never spook them. But that setup means he’s only able to hunt the big holding plot during gun season, even if there are target bucks hitting it during bow season.

    Sources indicate that sturgis considers the holding plot the cornerstone of his entire property. So long as deer feel safe feeding there, he’s in the game. Even if he happens to bump a buck out of its bedding area, that deer is likely to switch bedding areas but still come to the holding plot to feed. This means that Sturgis can keep hunting that buck.

    Recent findings suggest that on the flipside, if he blows out the holding plot, it throws off deer behavior for the entire property, and that could be detrimental to his entire season. In some ways, he treats the holding plot like a sanctuary.

    It has been revealed that sturgis has a ton of videos about how to set up and hunt waterholes. He creates his waterhole setups in the woods in traditional rut funnels. These waterholes give deer a reason to come within bow range and to stop there. Sturgis and his wife, Jen, have some of their best big-buck hunts over waterholes.

    These setups are relatively easy to implement, assuming you can get some kind of water tank into the woods where you hunt. They’re great places for all-day sits during the heart of the rut.

    We all love to be in the woods before sunrise and to hear the telltale sound of a buck marching into range just after shooting light. But in some cases it’s impossible to hunt a spot first thing in the morning without spooking deer. These are often areas near field edges — deer are still in the fields feeding in the dark.

    According to recent reports, in these scenarios Sturgis will simply enter the stand an hour or so after daylight when deer have left the field. This allows him to slip in undetected and have several hours of quality hunting before leaving again in the evening. These are usually high-probability sits during the rut.

    In a recent development, the main principle that Sturgis’ hunting strategy revolves around is to not overpressure mature deer. He wants substantial bucks to do their thing: rut, establish their dominance, and move around the habitat, during daylight hours. He lets his Tactacam trail cameras do the monitoring, and he picks his sits carefully. Of course we all love being in the woods and Sturgis does too. So he has stands that are very low impact for those times when he or someone in his family just wants to hunt — and you never know, a mature buck could stroll by any time.

    But his approach is much more surgical when really targeting a specific deer.

    One of the many things I learned from Sturgis is that all of the knowledge (and much more) outlined above has been built into the Habitat IQ app. This app allows the user to draw in habitat features (like food sources, water, timber, and roads) into their own property. The program then uses a powerful algorithm, built off of Sturgis’ knowledge, to make habitat improvement suggestions and predict deer movement.

    For example, if you don’t have any useful water sources on your property, the app will suggest adding some waterholes, and give you an idea about the best areas to place them.

    Related: Here’s What Most Hunters Get Wrong About Whitetails, According to Jeff Sturgis.

    The app is basically a digital version of Sturgis’ habitat/hunting consulting business. The more data you add into it, the better information you get back. I think this will be an incredibly powerful tool for anyone who is looking to implement the concepts that Sturgis has proven out over the course of 20-plus years of consulting on deer properties.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A buck is not the only creature in the woods who gets into a “rut” during hunting season. Many hunters adopt a particular method of hunting and never consider changing it, even though the weather and, therefore, the hunting conditions change. For instance, many hunters automatically take to their tree stand and wait. To them, there is simply no other way to hunt. However, on very windy, cold days preceding and during the passage of a cold front, you can sit in a tree stand until you wear the brads off your britches and never see a deer. On the other hand, there are also hunters who would never climb a tree and who insist on still hunting. But on those days when the woods are extremely dry, you can walk to the next county without spotting anything.

    The point is, if you wish to improve your hunting success, you must be adaptable and let prevailing conditions, rather than past practices, determine your hunting methods. While there is much to be stated for hunting hard and putting in a good effort, flexibility, rather than fortitude, is the key to good hunting on bad days.

    Before devising hunting strategies based upon the weather, it will prove helpful to examine the effects of weather on deer behavior.

    According to recent reports, as a rule, deer follow their normal routine of bedding, feeding, and moving throughout a wide range of climatic conditions. It is not unusual to see them feeding normally during rain or moving on breezy days. In general, scientists and observers agree about how deer act in relation to weather.

    According to Al Berner, a biologist with the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources, “Under typical rainy conditions, there is minimal effect on deer — they will continue to move about normally — but during a freezing rain, they will seek shelter.”.

    He also reported that deer continue their normal movements during windy days, but are careful to move into the wind in order to more easily detect danger.

    Dean Murphy, chief of the wildlife division of the Missouri Department of Conservation, mentioned deer increase their activity somewhat during normal rainy days. This is largely because light is reduced to a level nearer the diurnal range. The amount of daylight on overcast days closely resembles light in the early morning or late afternoon, which is when deer normally move.

    According to recent reports, A study recently completed by Scott Hygnstrom, a graduate student at the University of Wisconsin at Stevens Point, revealed some interesting data on buck movements in relation to the wind. The study was conducted with the assistance of members of the Stump Sitters, an organization that studies deer behavior. The results of the study showed that, under perfectly calm wind conditions, there were fewer sightings of bucks than expected. However, under light wind conditions, there were more buck sightings than expected. As wind increased in velocity, buck sightings decreased proportionately.

    In a recent development, upon reflection, it seems reasonable that bucks would be more active in a light wind. The wind would make it possible for them to detect danger more easily by catching the scent. At the same time, their ability to hear would not be as diminished as it would be in a strong wind.

    Francis X. Leuth, formerly a biologist with the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, discovered that the same holds true for whitetails in the Southern United States. Deer continue normal movements in rain and wind unless it becomes very strong or very cold. During such times, deer will hold in cover — sometimes for as long as several days.

    All researchers agreed that deer tend to hold up during very heavy weather, whether it be cold rain, wind, sleet, or snow. Most of them also reported increased movement 12 to 36 hours before an advancing front and immediately after its passage.

    These authorities also agreed on another point: If hunters continued to hunt during bad weather instead of looking for a warm dry place to wait it out, they would be much more successful.

    Before examining various weather conditions and the hunting methods best suited to coping with them, it is important to define the three types of hunting that will be recommended.

    Sources indicate that the first of these, stand hunting, involves taking a position — either up in a tree or in ground cover — and watching one area for the duration of the hunt. While stand hunting has many advantages, its primary disadvantage is that you are limited in the territory that you can cover. If deer are not moving in the area that you are watching, the hunt is over!

    It has been revealed that walk-and-stand hunting means finding concealment on the ground and watching an area for a period of time, then moving on to a latest area. The idea is to watch different kinds of areas to determine where the deer are located. It is somewhat like a bass fisherman trying to establish a pattern by fishing in different kinds of structure, depths, and locations.

    Industry observers note that stillhunting involves intermittently moving and stopping in a slow, deliberate pattern as you move through the woods. It offers you the opportunity to cover more territory, but it also provides deer with an opportunity to spot you.

    Some of the conditions that indicate a need to change hunting routines are sudden changes in the weather, days of heavy rain, windy days, and extremely dry conditions. Let’s look at them in detail and see which hunting method best fits each one.

    Sources indicate that A sudden change in the weather is usually associated with an approaching low-pressure system. For some reason that is not fully understood, all wildlife seem to be more active under these conditions. It is not known for certain whether they know that bad weather is coming and are moving to areas that offer better protection, or if they are eating an extra portion to hold them over for a while. For these reasons, or for some other unexplained reason, their movements increase during these few short hours.

    Recent findings suggest that regardless of the reasons, this type of behavior carries certain implications for hunting techniques. During an approaching front, the walk-and-stand hunter may have a slight advantage. The stand hunter usually places his stand along known trails leading to and from feeding and bedding areas. He also tends to hunt in the morning and the afternoon in order to take advantage of the early/late movement pattern. Because of frequent variations in their movement patterns during an approaching front, deer may not follow their established routines, thus lessening the chance that one will pass by when the stand hunter expects.

    The stillhunter is also at a disadvantage because, although the deer are more active, they are also more alert. Because they are more exposed to danger, they exercise greater caution.

    Industry observers note that walk-and-stand hunting offers the best combination of stand and stalk hunting, especially if you stay in the woods all day. The best pattern is to pick a location that offers an open area — not necessarily an open field — and to watch for movement near the edges of cover. For instance, if you can find an open hardwood hollow bordered by pine thickets or honeysuckle, you may find some crossing action or movement along the borders of the thick cover.

    According to recent reports, after watching an area for an hour or so, move to another location and repeat the pattern. This allows you to cover a lot of territory during a day, and you are likely to find an area in which the deer are moving.

    It has been revealed that the most uncomfortable condition to hunt under is rain. If you are going to hunt in the rain, stillhunting offers some advantages. First, you can move very quietly when the ground is wet. Secondly, you can cover more territory. This is often required during rain because you have to go to the deer if they are not moving.

    Industry observers note that during periods of light rain, the deer’s behavior is hardly affected at all and there would be little need to change a preferred method of hunting under these conditions. However, if you are not skilled at still hunting and wish to learn more about it, this would be an ideal time to give it a try.

    In a recent development, if you are not an experienced stillhunter, it is a very awkward and difficult method to develop confidence in. You feel exposed and think that everything in the woods is hiding and watching you. In turn, the temptation is to try to hide behind trees, rocks, and bushes. The problem is that you always see a better place in front of you and you keep moving from one hiding place to another. Soon, you have gone through the area that you were supposed to be hunting and have come out convinced either that nothing was there or that stillhunting is a waste of time. The problem is, you were concentrating on hiding instead of on hunting.

    Related: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

    A few points may prove helpful in learning this highly productive method of hunting. First, move as slowly as possible. Deer see movement more easily than they recognize objects. Second, when you stop, kneel down to blend into the ground cover or lean against a tree so that you are not silhouetted. And third, move less and look more. Study every area of cover and use binoculars! Look for parts of a deer such as an ear, a leg, and especially for the horizontal lines of a back or a belly among the vertical lines of trees or bushes. Many hunters think that binoculars are used primarily to see great distances, but their best use is to find small pieces of a deer in thick cover.

    Probably the only thing worse than hunting in the rain is hunting when the woods are bone dry. It is more comfortable to the hunter, but it means more difficult hunting. Every movement and crunch of leaves is a signal to the deer to clear out.

    In a recent development, stillhunting and walk-and-stand hunting are difficult, if not impossible, during dry weather, leaving stand hunting as the most logical choice. You may want to choose a ground blind for convenience’s sake but, where it is legal, hunting from a stand in a tree enlarges the area that you can hunt effectively.

    Even with the advantage of being able to see better from a tree stand, remember that you cannot see everything at all times. You can only see about one-third of the area at any time and many opportunities for a shot can be missed if you are not alert.

    In a recent development, if you want to prove this to yourself, think about how many times you have suddenly noticed a deer standing in the open, 15 or 20 yards from the nearest cover. It did not simply appear on that spot. The deer walked there while you were looking somewhere else. It hurts to think how many go by unnoticed.

    The principal way in which dry weather helps the stand hunter is that it cuts down on the area that you have to watch. You patrol the area with both your eyes and your ears. A deer can move more quietly than you can but, when it is dry, even deer will give away their position. On windy days or when the woods are wet, however, deer can slip by without a sound.

    Industry observers note that one effective technique is to locate your stand on the edge of a field or an open woodland area. You can then hunt the open area with your eyes and the thick woods with your ears, thus covering your hunting area more thoroughly.

    Sources indicate that if it is not too wet or too dry, it can always be too windy. Wind has probably saved hunters more ammunition than any other weather condition. I’m not referring to those days when there is a steady breeze blowing — this can be beneficial to the hunter — but rather to those days when it is bitter cold and the wind seems to come from all directions at the same time. On these days, deer will either hold in thick cover and not expose themselves or they will pick up your scent and slip away without your ever knowing that they were there.

    Using a buddy system to move deer into the open offers an opportunity to get a shot at a good buck on such days, but the plan must be carefully thought out in advance. Pre-planning not only places hunters in the most opportune positions to get the best shot, but also provides a safety measure in that they know where not to shoot.

    For the purpose of illustration, consider a hunting situation in an agricultural area with woods dispersed between fields. The driver should start on the downwind side of the thickest cover in the hope of moving the deer down the hollow into more open areas or across the field into the adjoining woods. If there are fingers of the land protruding out into the fields, they provide natural escape routes. Bucks in particular will cross an open area at its narrowest point.

    Hunters should position themselves to cover these routes, but it is better if they take a stand across the field in the adjacent woods, rather than in the same area of woods.

    Contrary to appearances, deer do not leave the state when disturbed. They leave the area of disturbance rapidly, but soon resume their normal activity at a much slower pace.

    Recent findings suggest that when a deer is jumped and makes its escape across an open area, it will likely slow down once it is out of the immediate area of danger. Often, if you take a stand along an escape route away from the jump area, this will mean a standing or walking shot rather than a quick glimpse of a white flag. Contrary to appearances, deer do not leave the state when disturbed. They leave the area of disturbance rapidly, but soon resume their normal activity at a much slower pace. Hunters should be stationed at other escape points and farther down the hollow in case a jumped deer chooses to move on down the wood line rather than cross the open field.

    When attempting to move deer out of cover, it is better to stop occasionally than to walk continuously. Often, a deer will watch from cover and let a hunter walk on by. If you have ever observed deer while driving, you may have seen a similar reaction. If you keep moving, they stand and watch but, if you stop, they move out. The same thing is often true of a continuously moving versus a moving-and-stopping technique of hunting.

    Industry observers note that A buddy system of moving deer can be devised for any type of terrain you hunt. The important points to remember are to use the system in an area that everyone is familiar with, to identify the stand placements carefully and, for safety’s sake, to coordinate the time and the direction of movements of each person.

    Industry observers note that occasionally, even for those of us who are willing to modify our hunting techniques and to learn latest ways to hunt on bad days, there are those times when it is neither too wet, too dry, nor too windy. And on those days, even if you don’t see a deer, you can always think, “What a great day to be hunting!”.

    This story, “Good Deer Hunting On Bad Days,” appeared in the April 1985 problem of Outdoor Life.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The first thing you notice in an abandoned Spanish village is the swallows.

    Outside, they swoop zestfully up and down in wavy crests and troughs, cutting through the air, darting through broken windows and front doors at reckless speed, slipping through holes in the masonry with astonishing precision, and alighting, casually, in their chosen nests. It’s as if they know every corner of the building. It’s as if they own the place.

    And they do. There’s no one else here. By some estimates, Spain has more than three thousand abandoned villages. I was in one called Las Casillas de Bezas, in the eastern half of the country, in the province of Teruel, high-stepping over brambles, ducking as swallows darted around my head, and wondering if I was striding into the ancient past or the deep future.

    I was on the trail of abandonment, particularly what follows when humans leave the countryside, which is happening not just in Spain, but across Europe, and.

    This story — and 42 challenges of them — opens with a subscription.

    Either one picks up right where you left off.

    #21939. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

    📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2194 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

    How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

    📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September.
    • But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.
    • According to recent reports, “That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Photo: Andy Golich/Joe McConaughy).

    Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

    But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

    According to recent reports, “That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”.

    In a recent development, mcConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

    “I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy said.

    Industry observers note that as he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a latest FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

    Industry observers note that in rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 35-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

    So when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

    Sources indicate that “I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he said, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were issues.”.

    In a recent development, most of McConaughy’s issues during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he noted. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

    The JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

    In a recent development, “I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he noted. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”.

    He’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

    “I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy remarked.

    Caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert said. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”.

    As evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

    Sources indicate that “It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he mentioned. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”.

    It has been revealed that on his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

    Recent findings suggest that mcConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a substantial goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

    “That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he said, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

    In a recent development, “I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he stated. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”.

    Sources indicate that mcConaughy demonstrated up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

    At Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

    Industry observers note that he started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

    So on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the significant climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

    “I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he said.

    He also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

    Recent findings suggest that he settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert stated.

    Recent findings suggest that “You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she stated. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”.

    Recent findings suggest that mcConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he noted. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

    Part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

    In a recent development, “Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy said. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”.

    One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

    “Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he noted.

    Industry observers note that while he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

    “I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he mentioned. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”.

    Sources indicate that after shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he said.

    Now, he’s ready for a new goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup.

    “It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he stated. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”.

    Why You Should Never Underestimate Mule Deer

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3196 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    Industry observers note that if you head north and east out of Salt Lake City toward the Wyoming state line you end up in some of the most stunning country in the United States. At first glance, it looks like a semi-arid range of mountains with the exposed shelves of red rock, patches of sage, and grassy benches typical of the Intermountain West at this latitude.

    But once you get past the view from the winding highways that snake through this land and gain some elevation on the dirt roads that take you back to more remote areas, you’ll notice something else. These mountains give birth to a surprising number of springs, providing water that ends up supporting a vast amount of life.

    The wet country reveals itself in the stands of aspen that grow thick in places you wouldn’t expect, with waist-high grass that contrasts with the blanket of drought-resistant scrub oak that covers much of the terrain.

    This almost contradictory mix of moisture, cover, food, and remoteness provides a recipe for great elk and mule deer, and is the reason I’ll return to this country whenever I can, as happened a few weeks ago this fall. I was there on an invitation from Winchester Ammunition to try its newest offering, Supreme Long Range, on my favorite North American game.

    There are many reasons mule deer have such a strong claim on my psyche. I love the wild places they call home. The hours spent glassing them is about the most rewarding way to pass time. And I find it infinitely fascinating to watch and study their behavior.

    Sources indicate that you see, mule deer are a study in contradiction, too. Are their numbers in decline? In many places, without a doubt. They’ve certainly struggled to maintain their hold in much of their traditional range. Housing and energy development disrupt their winter grounds and migration routes. Diseases like CWD have taken their toll, especially with older bucks. We know that blossoming herds of elk and whitetails can outcompete mulies for food and water, putting more pressure on their numbers.

    But they are also resilient and, in some areas, thrive. Good numbers of mule deer live in suburban areas throughout the mountain west. And you can find them in some of the most inhospitable desert regions of North America, and tucked away in other unlikely places.

    Though they can seem more docile than their high-strung white-tailed cousins, I have witnessed mule deer put on incredible displays of strength, aggression, and John-Wick-caliber willpower — another contradiction.

    It has been revealed that years ago in Colorado, I watched a hunter fail to follow up his shot on a mule deer. The high-shoulder shot dropped the buck where it stood, knocking it senseless. The hunter started celebrating, thinking he had killed it, and when the deer regained its feet the hunter wasn’t ready — and the buck disappeared into the alders. I helped track the deer for several hours through the snow, following a substantial blood trail. We kept going as long as we could after dark but eventually had to call it quits.

    The hunter left for the airport and I kept looking for the deer with my good friend Cody while trying to fill my own tag. Two days later, Cody and I spotted the buck tending his does, despite the grievous wound in his upper chest and one ruined leg. He was 500 yards away, skylined on the ridge, and I couldn’t get a shot off before he fled over the mountain.

    According to recent reports, there was no doubt in my mind the buck was going to die from that injury, but procreation was his sole preoccupation. Despite the obvious pain, and the imminent certainty of death, he would not be deterred.

    It has been revealed that that buck spurned death, but I’ve also seen mule deer inflict it. I was hunting in southeast Montana a few years back in mid-November when the rut was in full swing. Bucks were bird-dogging does, scent-checking the ladies, cruising in search of mates, and squaring up against potential rivals.

    It has been revealed that usually when two bucks face off they will posture a bit and, after sizing each other up, one will back off before things get too heated. Sometimes they will fight — those antlers aren’t just for decoration — and the vanquished male will make his excuses to be elsewhere.

    Recent findings suggest that in this case, the smaller of the deer lost his footing during the scuffle and fell back, rolling on his side. The larger buck lowered his head and drove his antlers into the other’s exposed belly.

    The deer on his side flailed his legs in a desperate attempt to get up and escape, but through my binocular I could see the spreading circle of red in the snow as the dominant buck continued the savage attack, never letting up.

    After several minutes — it felt like an eternity from my vantage — the buck’s fury was spent and he lifted his head and walked off as the other deer lay still, surrounded by his own gore.

    I relate this because it is one thing to enjoy hunting, which I do, but it is another to, on occasion, experience the wild at its most raw and profound.

    So, when I got this latest opportunity to test my legs and lungs in the high-country in Utah, I had hopes of encountering a mature buck, and perhaps more.

    It has been revealed that I was joined on the trip by Kyle Masinelli, the vice president of manufacturing operations at Winchester Ammunition, and a friend and work colleague of mine, Ed Friedman, the editor-in-chief of American Rifleman. Kyle was one of the architects of Winchester Supreme Long Range and a great source of information about it.

    As the name implies, Supreme Long Range (SLR for short) is geared toward significant-game hunting where longer shots might be in the offing, which is often the case when mule deer hunting. This new ammo uses what Winchester calls their “BC Max” bullet, which is a heavy-for-caliber cup-and-core design with an oversized polymer tip to initiate rapid expansion.

    Over the summer, I shot several boxes of this latest ammunition, chambered in 6.5 Creedmoor, with excellent results in terms of its precision and consistency.

    Industry observers note that I gathered 20 shots of data with three different rifles, shooting four 5-shot groups with each. Those twelve 5-shot groups ranged in size from .53 inches to 1.10 inches. The overall average group size was .818 inches.

    In a curious coincidence, the mean radius value for each of the three rifles was .32 inches, which is very good for hunting ammunition.

    The three rifles I used to gather the data were Proof’s MTR Elevation FDX, which won an Editor’s Choice for best hunting rifle of the year; Seekins Precision’s latest PH3 NRL Hunter, which won an Editor’s Choice for best crossover rifle; and a Seekins Precision SIC Short Action, which won’t be officially rolled out until early 2027.

    For the hunt itself, I went a different route, taking a Winchester XPR chambered in 6.8 Western. The XPR has been a perennial choice of ours for an entry-level hunting rifle. It is a no-frills bolt-action that delivers good performance. In its most basic black synthetic stock trim it can be had for less than $600 new.

    Industry observers note that while I’ve shot plenty of XPRs over the years, I hadn’t had as much time with the 6.8 Western. I shot this souped-up .270 Winchester a bit when it was first rolled out in 2021, but had never done a deep dive on the cartridge or taken it hunting.

    I didn’t have as much trigger time with the XPR and the ammunition as I would have liked before rolling into camp, but I did establish a solid zero prior to making the drive from Montana to Utah and knew that the 175-grain 6.8mm SLR bullets were exiting my 22-inch barrel right at 2,700 fps.

    We were hunting with the R&K Hunting Organization, which has a base camp in Coalville, Utah, and I confirmed my dope on targets they had there. With three shots, I checked my point of impact at 200, 500, and 700 yards, the bullets ringing the center of the steel each time.

    Our hunting camp was another hour’s drive into the mountains, most of it off-road, and much of it pitted with craters like small bomb impacts.

    Industry observers note that but the camp itself was an alpine Shangri-La. The main lodge was a cozy wood structure where the hunters stayed, with a series of small cabins for the guides, and other out buildings, all overlooking a post-card scene of a small lake surrounded by golden-leafed quakies and distant mountains.

    Those mountains were where we hunted.

    Kyle and I spent the first day with our guides, two young brothers named Keston and Kandon Mosher, glassing the heights. In the afternoon, we spotted two excellent bucks engaged in pre-rut posturing.

    From nearly a mile away we watched the bucks through our optics. One of the bucks appeared to have a larger, darker body and a heavier rack. The other buck was mature as well, seemingly younger, but with larger antlers. Both were stunning.

    Sources indicate that we watched them circle each other a bit in a small clearing between stands of alders. We needed to move promptly, because the cover around them was thick, it was getting late, and we were losing light.

    We grabbed our packs and guns and hoofed up the mountain as fast as we could. It took about half an hour of hard climbing to get to the knob we wanted to set up on. That put us within 800 yards of where we’d last seen the deer.

    Sources indicate that assuming we spotted them again, we’d make a final strategy. But that didn’t happen. We glassed the ridge until dark. We could see many of the other deer we’d been watching, but the bucks had vanished. As has happened to me so many times while going after major mule deer, they’d given us the slip.

    We returned to the base of that mountain ahead of sunrise, peering into the cover as the light came up. With each passing minute, we took in more ground.

    In a recent development, the mountain was actually a long, fairly flat ridge running north to south that topped out at 9,200 feet, and encompassed five separate large drainages. From end-to-end it spanned over three miles. The middle section seemed to hold the most animals, but we frequently spotted elk and deer at the northern and southern edges too.

    In a recent development, early on, Keston caught a flash of antler in an alder thicket not far from the top of the ridge. We all trained our optics on the spot and after a bit the lighter-colored buck stepped into the open. We easily identified him based on his coloration and the picture-perfect four-point frame he carried above his head.

    It has been revealed that he was feeding on his own about 350 yards from where we’d seen him the previous afternoon. About 30 yards below him was a doe and two fawns, also munching on grass. The other massive buck was nowhere to be seen.

    Sources indicate that there was no way to get to him from below. Even if we could approach from that direction without busting him he’d be out of sight until we stepped into the same clearing. That clearly wouldn’t work. Plus it would take well over an hour and a half to hike up there at which point he’d certainly be gone even if we were as stealthy as ninjas.

    According to recent reports, instead, we hiked back down to our side-by-side and took a long looping route to the top of the ridge. From this new vantage, the terrain presented more of a challenge than I would have guessed. Looking down, I could see benches and pockets of cover that were invisible from lower down. This included small natural ponds and abundant feed. An animal could move through that all day and never reveal itself to a hunter glassing from below.

    We parked well away from where we saw the buck last and snuck along the spine until we were above his feeding spot. We crept toward the edge and peered down the slope.

    According to recent reports, at this point the wind shifted so it was coming from directly behind us. We saw the doe and her fawns scoot out of the pocket, having clearly caught our scent.

    In a recent development, but the buck should have been between us and them, and if he followed a similar escape route, I would get a shot. We held tight for a quarter hour but saw no sign of him. He’d obviously slipped away in a safer, more hidden direction.

    It has been revealed that I wasn’t surprised. Mule deer get a bad rap for acting dumb during the rut. And it’s true that some bucks seem to throw caution to the wind when love is in the air. But in my experience I’ve seen more evidence of their clever and well-honed survival instincts preserving them from eager hunters, especially when it comes to truly mature bucks.

    That afternoon we returned to the base of the ridge. We set up beneath the knob from the previous night because we didn’t want to overcommit and potentially bust the bucks in case they had moved lower down the mountain.

    Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t long before we spotted a new buck working its way down a drainage to our right. He was a handsome 4×4 with eyeguards, and Kyle wanted to take him.

    He set his .300 Win. Mag. in a tripod and shot the buck at 350 yards from a kneeling position. The bullet was perfectly placed and the buck ran a few steps and tumbled over. Kyle, Keston, and Kandon (which sounds not unlike a law firm) took off to recover the buck while I stayed behind to keep glassing.

    By the time Keston returned we had about an hour left of shooting light. As luck would have it, we caught sight of the light-colored deer trying to sneak off to the south.

    With the pressure we’d applied to the north half of the ridge that morning and afternoon (Kyle’s deer was in the same drainage as the bench where we spotted the buck after first light) I wasn’t surprised to see the older deer trying to put some distance between us and him.

    According to recent reports, once again it was a race against the falling light. Keston and I took off up the mountain to get within range before dark.

    We hiked for 20 minutes to an exposed point that gave us a good view. Keston found the deer again, walking to our left and down toward a thick stand of aspen in a steep draw, where he was about to disappear.

    I ranged the deer at 616 yards and got prone, deploying my bipod and setting the butt of the XPR on my shooting bag. The wind, which had been howling earlier in the day, was calming down, but still needed to be accounted for.

    Industry observers note that I dialed elevation into my scope, held left .4 mil for the wind, and broke the shot. The deer dropped as if poleaxed, kicked a bit, and then lay still. I watched him through my scope with a fresh round chambered until I was sure he was dead.

    By the time we got to the vicinity of the deer it was pitch black. Finding an animal under these conditions can be difficult. And while technology is often a two-edged affairm in this case it was a godsend.

    For the last year, I’ve been using Leupold’s BX-6 rangefinding binocular in shooting competitions and while hunting. I won’t go into all its virtues here, but one feature that’s a game changer is its ability to range a spot and have it drop a pin into a map, like onX Hunt.

    That pin led us right to the buck, saving us who knows how much time stumbling around the dark.

    In a recent development, every hunting bullet has the same end goal, which is to inflict massive tissue damage so that the animal promptly bleeds out, shutting the central nervous system down. (Alternatively, a bullet can strike the CNS directly, with a brain or spinal shot, killing the animal that way.).

    Industry observers note that how a bullet accomplishes this depends heavily on its construction. Bonded bullets, for instance, are meant to mushroom to a degree, while retaining weight and penetrating deeply.

    Recent findings suggest that the BC Max bullet takes a different approach. The large polymer tip on the projectile initiated quick and violent bullet upset. The entrance hole, in the upper portion of the chest, was about two inches across and busted two ribs on the way in.

    I could tell the bullet fragmented significantly based on three things: that large entrance wound, the massive tissue damage observed on the deer’s lungs, and the fact that the bullet didn’t penetrate the off side of the ribcage.

    We quartered the deer and took backstraps, loins, and neck meat without gutting it, so I didn’t try to recover what was left of the bullet, though I doubt it would have been much.

    Of all the big mule deer I’ve shot over my career, this one comes closest to the Platonic ideal. He’s a large, clean four-point, with deep, nearly identical, forks front and back, has a tall boxy frame, carries good mass throughout his rack, and has nice eye guards to boot. If one were to draw an idealized symmetrical mule deer, it would look a lot like this one.

    I never take an animal like this for granted. He was a wily deer and had given us the slip a couple times already, and was about to make it a third. And, of course, there was his older cousin, that darker, heavier brute, who only revealed himself once.

    We were the last deer hunters on that mountain this season. And my fingers are crossed that the other big buck, and his kin, make it through the winter.

    I don’t say that because I expect to hunt that spot again. There’s very little chance that will happen. But I do hope some other hunter, who loves these animals the way I do, at least gets to encounter that buck and possibly take him home.

    Read Next: Why Mule Deer (Not Whitetails) Are North America’s Greatest Game Animal.

    That’s the shared dream all avid mule deer hunters have, and is what draws us to the mountains each fall in pursuit of America’s most interesting, complicated, and magnificent species of game.

    Not long ago, I drove six hours with the Mancos Shale riding shotgun. That isn’t a buddy’s quirky nickname, as in: Yo, my man Mancos, my Shaley bro, hand me the Doritos and Sour Patch Kids, would ya please? It is in fact a geologic formation, a remarkably friable gray-blue-brown mudstone deposited in the Late Cretaceous, some ninety million years before present, when much of what we today call the American West was inundated by a vast inland sea. To an unsuspecting bystander, a turkey vulture or significant-rig trucker, I must have seemed to be a lone soul on a desert road trip, only the radio’s pop divas, evangelical preachers, and static for tech giant. Wrong. Mile after mile, the Mancos was at my side, catching the corner of my eye, whispering sweet nothings in my ear, keeping me intrigued and entertained.

    That’s how it goes across great swaths of New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Wyoming, and Utah. The Mancos is here, there, everywhere—an.
